label: Explain a science topic
brief: A short class presentation explaining how photosynthesis turns sunlight into food, with one everyday example that makes it stick.
title: Solar Powered Sugar
script:
## [HOOK] · ~25s
Imagine a world where you don't have to go to the dining hall or pack a lunch because you can just **stand in the sun** and feel your stomach fill up. No cooking, no shopping, no chewing. Just light. That's exactly what every blade of grass and towering oak tree does every single second.

## [PROBLEM] · ~25s
Plants can't just eat soil. Dirt is mostly minerals and decayed matter, not energy. If a plant couldn't manufacture its own fuel, it would wither in days. Without this one specific process, the entire food chain collapses. No plants mean no herbivores, which means **zero** food for us.

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~35s
Here's how it works. Plants use a pigment called chlorophyll to catch sunlight, which acts like a spark. They take in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the roots. Then, they use that solar energy to break those molecules apart and rebuild them into **glucose**. That's a simple sugar that serves as the plant's primary food source.

> *(pause)*

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~25s
Think of it like a solar-powered kitchen. The sunlight is the **stove**, the water and air are the raw ingredients, and the glucose is the finished meal. When you eat a crisp apple or a piece of celery, you're literally eating stored sunlight that the plant cooked up weeks ago. *(slow down here)* It's bottled energy.

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~25s
Next time you're walking across campus, look at the leaves. Don't just see green; see **factories**. Try to spot which plants are getting the most light and realize they're working the hardest to build sugar. Start thinking of every green space as a massive, silent power plant fueling the planet.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~15s
We don't have the luxury of standing in the sun to get full. But we get to eat the results of that process every day. Remember, every bite you take started as **pure light**.

## [QUESTIONS] · ~10s
I'm sure some of you have thoughts on how this works in the dark.

> **Ask the room:** "Who wants to take a crack at that?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: Pitch your research project
brief: Pitch my final-year research project on how sleep affects exam performance to my professors: the question, the method, and why it matters.
title: Sleep And Scores
script:
## [HOOK] · ~25s
Imagine a student who's spent **forty hours** a week in the library. They've memorized every page and mastered every formula. But the night before the final, they pull an all-nighter to cram one last chapter. They walk into that hall feeling focused, but their brain is actually operating at the level of someone who's **legally drunk**.

## [PROBLEM] · ~25s
We've treated the all-nighter as a rite of passage for years. But the cost isn't just a few yawns in the back row. When we starve the brain of sleep, we don't just get tired; we lose the ability to **retrieve** information. A student can know the answer, but they simply can't find it under pressure.

> *(pause)*

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~50s
My research proves that sleep isn't just rest; it's where the actual learning happens. First, I'm looking at how sleep stabilizes memories. Think of it like hitting the **save button** on a document; if you pull the plug too early, the data is gone. Then, I'm measuring the impact on executive function. This is the part of the brain that handles complex problem-solving and critical thinking. If that's offline, a student can't apply what they know to a new question. Finally, I'm tracking the precise tipping point where losing a few hours of sleep leads to a **measurable drop** in GPA.

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~40s
Look at the difference between two students. One sleeps six hours; the other sleeps three. On a simple multiple-choice test, they might look the same. But give them an essay that requires synthesis and logic, and the gap widens. The sleep-deprived student starts looping. They write the same sentence three times because their brain has lost the **thread**. *(slow down here)* It's not a lack of knowledge. It's a failure of the hardware.

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~25s
I need your approval to track **fifty students** over the next two finals cycles. I'll use wearable sleep trackers and correlate that data with their raw scores. It's a tight loop of data that moves us past the anecdote and into **hard evidence** about how we study.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~15s
We can't keep letting students walk into exams with brains that are essentially **blacked out**. It's time to stop praising the all-nighter and start prioritizing the save button.

## [QUESTIONS] · ~10s
I'm ready to walk through the specific tracking metrics if you're curious.

> **Ask the room:** "Who here actually feels they performed their best after an all-nighter?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: Give a team update
brief: A quick quarterly team update: what we shipped, one number that moved, the blocker we need help with, and what's next.
title: Quarterly Velocity Update
script:
## [HOOK] · ~25s
We didn't just hit the target this quarter. We **broke** it. While the rest of the organization was bracing for a plateau, we pushed the release cycle from fourteen days down to **six**. That's not a marginal gain. It's a complete shift in how we deliver value to the customer.

## [PROBLEM] · ~25s
But speed is dangerous if you're moving in the wrong direction. Last month, we saw a **twelve percent** spike in critical bugs because our QA process couldn't keep up with the dev pace. That's lost revenue and frustrated users. We can't afford to trade stability for a faster clock.

> *(pause)*

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~35s
Here's the reality. We've proven we can build fast, so now we focus on building **right**. First, we're automating the regression suite to catch errors before they ship. Then, we're shifting our focus toward the API integration project. Finally, we're tightening the feedback loop between sales and engineering so we stop building features that nobody actually uses.

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~25s
Look at the Delta project. We shipped the core module in **three weeks** instead of two months. The client didn't just sign the renewal; they doubled their seat count because they saw the feature they asked for actually appearing in the product in **real-time**. *(slow down here)* That's the power of this pace.

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~25s
I need your help with the legal bottleneck. Our contract approvals are taking **ten days**, which kills our momentum. If you've got a direct line to the legal leads, I need you to push for a streamlined sign-off for low-risk updates. Let's get that approval window down to **forty-eight hours**.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~15s
We've already proven we can break the target on speed. Now, we're going to break the record for **reliability**. Let's keep that momentum moving into the next quarter.

## [QUESTIONS] · ~10s
I'm sure you've got thoughts on the legal bottleneck or the API shift.

> **Ask the room:** "Who's seen this friction elsewhere?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: Propose a new idea
brief: Propose replacing our weekly status meeting with a written update: the problem, the proposal, and a two-week trial to test it.
title: Ending Status Meetings
script:
## [HOOK] · ~~25s
Your calendar is a **wall** of back-to-back blocks. You spend four hours a week in status meetings just to hear that things are on track. Most of that time is spent waiting for the one update that actually matters to you, while the rest of the room listens to things they don't need to know.

## [PROBLEM] · ~~25s
It's a hidden tax on our **productivity**. When six executives sit in a room for an hour, we aren't spending one hour. We're spending six. That's a massive operational cost for information that could've been read in **three minutes** via an email or a shared doc before the day even started.

> *(pause)*

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~~35s
We need to move the update to a written format. First, we shift the reporting to a concise, asynchronous document where every lead lists only their blockers and wins. Then, we use the meeting time exclusively for **decision-making**. If there's nothing to decide, we don't meet. We stop reporting for the sake of reporting and start using our synchronous time for actual **strategy**.

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~~25s
I saw this work with a regional ops team last year. They killed their weekly sync and moved to a bulleted Friday update. They didn't lose a single beat on delivery. In fact, their output **increased** because the leads spent less time preparing slide decks and more time actually running their departments. *(slow down here)*

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~~25s
Let's test this for **two weeks**. Starting Monday, we cancel the status call. Instead, everyone submits a three-bullet update by Thursday afternoon. If we hit a wall or miss a critical update, we go back to the old way. But if it works, we just bought back **four hours** of our week.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~~15s
Stop staring at that wall of calendar blocks. Let's trade the performance of a status meeting for the **clarity** of a written page. It's a small shift that gives us our time back.

## [QUESTIONS] · ~~10s
I'm curious if anyone sees a specific risk in this trial.

> **Ask the room:** "Who's worried about what we might miss?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: Open a product demo
brief: Open a product demo for an app that turns voice memos into to-do lists: hook the room, show the problem, and set up the demo.
title: Voice To Action
script:
## [HOOK] · ~25s
Imagine you're driving home and a **brilliant** idea hits you. You record a quick voice memo. It's thirty seconds of rambling, excitement, and maybe a bit of traffic noise. You feel great. You've captured it. But then that recording just sits there. It's a digital graveyard where good ideas go to **die**.

## [PROBLEM] · ~25s
The cost isn't just a lost idea. It's the **mental tax** of knowing you have a list of recordings you're too exhausted to listen to. When you finally open that app, you don't see a plan. You see a wall of audio files. Most of us just **give up**.

> *(pause)*

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~35s
We don't need more ways to record our thoughts. We need a way to make those thoughts **useful**. That means stripping away the "ums" and the tangents to find the actual task. It means turning a rambling sentence into a clear, dated action item. And finally, it means pushing that task directly into your calendar so it **actually happens**.

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~25s
I tried this last week with a chaotic five-minute brain dump while walking the dog. Usually, that's a chore to transcribe. But the system tore through it. It ignored the dog barking and the side-tracks. It gave me **four clean tasks** and a deadline. *(speed up)* It took two seconds.

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~25s
Stop treating your voice memos like a diary. Start treating them like a **command center**. I want you to think of the last thing you recorded that you never actually did. Keep that specific task in your head while I show you how we're going to **fix it**.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~15s
No more digital graveyards. No more wasted brilliance. Let's stop recording things we'll never hear and start building a list that **actually moves**. Here is how it works.

## [QUESTIONS] · ~10s
I'll take your questions once we've seen the magic in action.

> **Ask the room:** "Who here has more than ten unlistened-to voice memos on their phone right now?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: Start a conference talk
brief: The opening of a talk on why small daily habits beat big resolutions, with a personal story as the hook.
title: Small Wins Habit
script:
## [HOOK] · ~25s
Three years ago, I spent an entire Sunday planning the **perfect** version of my life. I bought a new planner, cleared my desk, and wrote down ten massive goals that would change everything. By Tuesday afternoon, I'd missed every single one of them. I wasn't lazy. I was just **exhausted** by my own expectations.

## [PROBLEM] · ~25s
We've been taught that growth requires a giant leap. We wait for January first or a sudden burst of inspiration to overhaul our entire existence. But that's how we end up in a cycle of **shame**. When you set a mountain-sized goal and fail, you don't just lose the habit. You lose your **confidence** in your own word.

> *(pause)*

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~50s
I've started wondering if the secret isn't the leap, but the tiny, almost invisible step. It's the idea that a **one percent** shift is more sustainable than a hundred percent overhaul. Instead of trying to write a book, you just commit to one honest sentence a day. Instead of a grueling gym regime, you just put on your running shoes. When the requirement is that small, it's almost impossible to fail. That's where the magic happens. You stop fighting your own resistance and start building a **momentum** that actually lasts because it doesn't ask you to be a different person overnight.

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~40s
Think of it like sketching. If I try to paint a masterpiece in one go, I'll probably freeze up and ruin the canvas. *(slow down here)* But if I just draw one light line, then another, then a circle, the image eventually **emerges**. I tried this with reading. I stopped aiming for a book a week and aimed for **one page** a night. I ended up reading more in six months than I had in six years.

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~25s
Pick one thing you've been failing at. Now, shrink it. Shrink it until it feels **ridiculous**. If you want to meditate, do it for thirty seconds. If you want to clean the house, pick up **three things**. Do that one tiny thing tomorrow morning. Don't add anything else. Just prove to yourself that you can show up.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~15s
We don't need more grand plans or fancy planners to change our lives. We just need to stop staring at the mountain and start focusing on the **single step**. Forget the big resolution. Just find your one percent.

## [QUESTIONS] · ~10s
I'm curious if any of you have a small win that actually stuck. What's the tiniest habit that changed your day?

> **Ask the room:** "What's one tiny habit you've actually managed to keep?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: Give a wedding toast
brief: A warm toast at my best friend's wedding: how we met, one funny story, and a wish for the couple.
title: The Perfect Match
script:
## [HOOK] · ~~25s
Twenty years ago, I met a kid who thought he could convince me that a **half-eaten** ham sandwich was a delicacy. He didn't just lie; he sold it with a level of confidence that should've been illegal. I bought it, of course. That's how it started. Just me, a bad sandwich, and a lifelong friendship.

## [PROBLEM] · ~~25s
Now, we've all seen the versions of this guy who try to play it cool. The polished, put-together version standing here today. But I've spent two decades seeing the **chaos** behind the curtain. The guy who once tried to fix a leaky sink with duct tape and a prayer, nearly flooding an entire apartment complex.

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~~35s
But then he met her. Suddenly, the duct tape vanished and he actually started reading the manuals. He didn't change who he was, but he found someone who makes him want to be the **best** version of that chaos. She brings the calm to his storm, and he brings a spark to her life that makes everything a bit more colorful.

> *(pause)*

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~~25s
I remember the first time he told me about her. He didn't use the usual lines. He just looked at me, completely dazed, and admitted he'd finally found someone **smarter** than him. *(wry smile)* For those of us who know him, that was the first real sign that this was the one.

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~~25s
So, I'm asking everyone to stand up. Grab your glasses and make sure they're full. We're not just celebrating a wedding today. We're celebrating the fact that someone actually agreed to manage this man's **shenanigans** for the rest of eternity. Let's give them the welcome they deserve.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~~15s
To the happy couple. May your life together be full of love, laughter, and absolutely **zero** ham sandwiches. To the bride and groom. *(raise glass)* Cheers!

## [QUESTIONS] · ~~10s
I'm sure some of you have your own horror stories about the groom you'd like to share during the reception.

> **Ask the room:** "Who's got the best one?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: Introduce yourself
brief: Introduce myself at a community meetup: who I am, what I'm into, and what I'd love to learn from the people here.
title: Shared Curiosity
script:
## [HOOK] · ~25s
Imagine spending your entire weekend taking apart a broken toaster just to see if you can make it work again. *(slow down here)* That's how I've spent most of my adult life. I'm the person who can't look at a gadget or a process without wondering **why** it was built that way.

> *(pause)*

## [PROBLEM] · ~25s
The problem is that curiosity usually happens in a vacuum. You spend hours in your own head or staring at a screen, and you hit a wall. When you're the only person in the room interested in a niche topic, your growth **stops** the moment you run out of your own ideas.

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~30s
That's why I'm here. I'm driven by a love for building things from scratch and a bit of an obsession with how systems fit together. But more than that, I'm looking for the perspective I don't have. I want to find the gaps in my thinking and fill them with the weird, specific expertise you all carry.

> *(pause)*

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~25s
Last year, I tried to automate my entire garden using a few cheap sensors and a lot of hope. It failed **miserably** because I didn't understand basic soil chemistry. A ten-minute conversation with one gardener saved me six months of guessing. That's the kind of shortcut I'm looking for here.

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~25s
So, here's the plan. If you've mastered something that seems boring to you but looks like magic to everyone else, please tell me about it. Find me during the break and give me the **one-sentence** version of what you're obsessed with right now. I'll likely have a question.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~15s
I'm still that person who wants to take the toaster apart, but this time, I'd rather do it with a room full of people who actually know how the **wiring** works.

## [QUESTIONS] · ~10s
I'd love to hear from you now. Who wants to start?

> **Ask the room:** "What's the one thing you're an expert in that nobody ever asks you about?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: Tell me about yourself
brief: Answer 'Tell me about yourself' in a product designer interview: my background, one project I'm proud of, and why this role.
title: The Designer's Pitch
script:
## [HOOK] · ~25s
Most designers spend this part of the interview reciting a **resume**. They list the years, the tools, and the titles. But a resume is just a ledger of where I've been. What actually matters is the **value** I've left behind at every single one of those stops.

## [PROBLEM] · ~25s
The danger in design is falling in love with the **pixel** instead of the problem. I've seen teams spend six months polishing a feature that users didn't even want. That's not design. That's an **expensive** hobby. It wastes runway and kills momentum when the market is moving faster than your sprint cycle.

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~35s
I approach product work as a bridge between user pain and business growth. First, I strip away the assumptions to find the actual **friction** point. Once that's clear, I build a lean solution that solves the core need without adding bloat. Finally, I measure the result against the **bottom line**. It's a cycle of evidence, execution, and refinement.

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~25s
At my last firm, we had a checkout flow where **twenty percent** of users dropped off at the final screen. *(slow down here)* I didn't redesign the page. I removed two unnecessary form fields and clarified the pricing. We saw conversion jump by **five percent** in one week. Simple. Direct. Profitable.

> *(pause)*

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~25s
That's why I'm here. Your current product has a massive opportunity to scale its onboarding, and I've already identified **three specific** areas where we can cut friction. I want to apply that same ruthless prioritization to your roadmap starting on day one.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~15s
I'm not here to just make things look better. I'm here to make them **work** better. Let's stop reciting the resume and start talking about how we move your **metrics**.

## [QUESTIONS] · ~10s
I've given you the highlight reel, but I'm sure you've got some specific gaps you want me to fill.

> **Ask the room:** "Where should we start?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: A challenge you overcame
brief: Answer 'Tell me about a challenge you overcame' with a clear story: the situation, what I did, and the result.
title: Ownership Over Blame
script:
## [HOOK] · ~~25s
We've all been in that meeting. The one where a **critical bug** hits production on a Friday afternoon, and the first thing everyone does is point fingers. People don't look for the fix. They look for the person to blame so they can protect their own reputation before the weekend starts.

## [PROBLEM] · ~~25s
I lived this three years ago when a deployment wiped a client's database. The cost wasn't just the **four hours** of downtime. It was the trust. My team stopped communicating because they were terrified of being the one to take the fall. We weren't solving problems. We were managing optics.

> *(pause)*

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~~35s
The only way out of that cycle is a culture of absolute ownership. It starts by decoupling the error from the person. You focus on the **systemic failure** that allowed the mistake to happen rather than the hand that clicked the button. Once you remove the fear of punishment, you get the truth. And the truth is the only thing that lets you build a permanent fix.

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~~25s
I stopped the finger-pointing by owning the failure myself, even though I didn't write the code. *(slow down here)* I led a blameless post-mortem where we mapped every single point of failure. We didn't find a scapegoat. We found a **gap in our staging environment** and patched it within forty-eight hours.

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~~25s
Next time a project hits a wall, don't ask who messed up. Ask what **safety net** was missing. Change the question from "who did this" to "how did the system allow this." It's a small shift in phrasing, but it changes how your best engineers behave when things go wrong.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~~15s
Stop looking for the person to blame. Start looking for the gap in the process. That's how you move from a culture of fear to a culture of **performance**.

> *(pause)*

## [QUESTIONS] · ~~10s
I'm curious if any of you have tried this approach in your own teams.

> **Ask the room:** "Has a blameless culture actually worked for you?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: Talk about your hometown
brief: Describe my hometown to new friends in simple, natural English: where it is, what it's famous for, and my favourite place there.
title: My Hidden Gem
script:
## [HOOK] · ~~25s
Imagine a place where the streets smell like **roasted coffee** and the hills are so steep you'll actually feel your calves burning just walking to the store. It's a tiny dot on the map tucked away in the mountains, but it's got a personality that's way too big for its zip code.

## [PROBLEM] · ~~25s
Most people just drive right past us on the highway. They miss out on the **best** sourdough in the state and a community that actually knows their neighbors' names. If you stick to the tourist maps, you're basically seeing a cardboard cutout of the real town.

> *(pause)*

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~~30s
You've gotta see the old clock tower first because it's the town's heartbeat. Then you need to hit the riverside market where the locals haggle over handmade quilts. Finally, you have to visit the hidden bookstore under the bridge. It's the only place I know where the books are **cheaper** than the coffee.

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~~25s
Last summer, I took a friend there who hated "small towns." Within two hours, he was sitting on a curb eating a giant cinnamon roll and asking if he could **move** there. *(wry smile)* He didn't move, obviously, but the cinnamon roll won him over.

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~~25s
If you're free this weekend, I'm driving up there. Pack a bag, leave the fancy shoes at home, and come with me. I'll show you the shortcut to the river that takes **ten minutes** instead of an hour. You just have to say yes.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~~15s
So, forget the highway and the tourist maps. Come see the steep hills and the roasted coffee for yourself. I promise those **burning calves** are totally worth the view.

## [QUESTIONS] · ~~10s
I'm sure you've got questions about the food or the hiking trails. What's on your mind?

> **Ask the room:** "Who's coming with me?"
> *(pause for responses)*

label: Monday small talk
brief: Everyday small talk in English: greeting a coworker on Monday, asking about their weekend, and sharing a little about mine.
title: Monday Morning Rituals
script:
## [HOOK] · ~25s
Imagine it's Monday morning. You're at the coffee machine. A coworker walks in, and for three seconds, you both just **stare** at each other. You know you should say something, but the words feel heavy. You don't want to be awkward, but you don't want to force a conversation that feels fake.

> *(pause)*

## [PROBLEM] · ~25s
Most of us treat small talk like a chore. We stick to the same boring scripts and end up sounding like robots. When you just say "fine" and move on, you're missing a chance to actually **connect**. That silence isn't just awkward; it's a wall that keeps your colleagues at a distance.

## [CORE MESSAGE] · ~30s
The secret is to move from a closed question to an open one. Instead of asking if their weekend was good, ask what the **highlight** of their weekend was. Once they answer, share a tiny, specific detail about your own time off. Maybe you tried a new bakery or finally finished a book. It's about trading facts for feelings.

> *(pause)*

## [PROOF/STORY] · ~25s
I used to be the "fine" person. Then I started asking people about their Sunday traditions. One coworker mentioned he spends every Sunday morning baking sourdough. Now, we don't just talk about the weather. We talk about **crust and crumb**. A five-second shift turned a stranger into a friend.

## [WHAT TO DO] · ~25s
Tomorrow, try one specific change. When you see that coworker, don't ask "how are you." Ask them for **one good thing** that happened over the break. Listen to the answer, find one detail to follow up on, and then share one small win from your own weekend. Keep it light. Keep it brief.

## [CLOSING LINE] · ~15s
Next time you're standing by that coffee machine, don't let the silence win. Stop staring and start asking. Turn those three seconds of awkwardness into a **real conversation**.

> *(slow down here)*

## [QUESTIONS] · ~10s
I'm curious if you have a go-to question that always works.

> **Ask the room:** "What's your best icebreaker for a Monday morning?"
> *(pause for responses)*
